analysis.one_liner: Ends the federal overtime exemption for truck drivers so they earn time-and-a-half past 40 hours.
analysis.headline: The bill to end truckers' overtime exemption was referred to committee in November 2023 and never received a hearing or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 1938, federal overtime law has excluded truck drivers covered by motor carrier rules, meaning they can work far beyond 40 hours a week with no required time-and-a-half pay. This one-sentence bill would delete that exemption, making motor carrier employees eligible for overtime like most other workers. It was introduced by Senator Padilla with five Democratic and Independent cosponsors in November 2023, referred to the Senate labor committee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.who_benefits: Roughly the nation's long-haul and motor carrier drivers, who today can be worked past 40 hours a week without any time-and-a-half pay. Repealing the exemption would give them the same federal overtime right most other hourly workers have, boosting pay for the long weeks typical in trucking and, at the margin, pushing carriers to spread work across more drivers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Truck drivers and motor carrier employees

how_it_helps.text: Repeals section 13(b)(1) of the Fair Labor Standards Act, the provision that since 1938 has exempted motor carrier employees from federal overtime pay.
After repeal, covered truck drivers would be entitled to time-and-a-half pay for hours worked beyond 40 in a week, the same as most other American workers.

analysis.who_pays: Trucking companies and motor carriers, which would owe time-and-a-half for hours over 40 in a week. Some of that cost would likely pass through to freight rates and consumer prices, and carriers might restructure schedules to limit overtime hours.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the exemption would raise labor costs for motor carriers, which could be passed on as higher freight and shipping costs that show up in consumer prices, and smaller carriers with thin margins could be squeezed hardest.

Trucking hours are already capped by separate motor-carrier safety rules rather than the standard 40-hour week, so applying the ordinary overtime framework to an industry with atypical schedules raises compliance and scheduling questions the bill, which is a single line repealing the exemption, does not address.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and targeted: millions of truck drivers, among the lowest-paid workers per hour worked in the country, would gain the right to time-and-a-half pay past 40 hours, a right most American workers have had for decades. The cost falls on carriers in a sector with thin margins and chronic driver turnover, and good-faith defenders of the exemption argue it would push up freight costs and complicate scheduling rules that treat driving hours differently from ordinary work hours. But the exemption dates to 1938, when the trucking industry looked nothing like it does today, and the bill did not receive even a committee hearing, so its merits were never publicly tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate labor committee in November 2023 and never came up again — no hearing, no vote — before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Padilla introduced the bill on November 9, 2023, joined by five Democratic and Independent colleagues.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the same day.
That was the bill's last recorded action: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote occurred before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
The bill itself was a single sentence repealing the FLSA provision that has exempted motor carrier employees from overtime since 1938.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Trucking carriers, who continue to pay no federal overtime to drivers regardless of hours worked. Nothing changed for drivers.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Trucking companies that avoid overtime pay

for.name: Alex Padilla
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.role: U.S. Senator (VT), Chair of the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor of the bill; as HELP Committee chair, did not bring the bill to a hearing or markup.

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or the Independent senator from Vermont, but no vote was ever taken and no opponent is named in the record, so the partisan shape of the opposition is unknown.

industries.note: Carriers have not had to pay federal overtime to drivers since 1938, so ending the exemption would raise their labor costs, especially for long-haul operations built around long weeks. For drivers, that same cost is the pay raise, so the industry's interest in this bill runs against the workers it employs.

industries.industry: Shippers and retailers dependent on freight
industries.note: Any overtime-driven increase in freight rates would flow through to the businesses that ship goods, and potentially to consumer prices. The size of the effect depends on how carriers adjust driver schedules and pay.
